topics.title: Coursework
topics.summary: King's does not ban AI, but the level allowed is set per assessment using four suggested levels: Minimal (spell/grammar checkers, transcription), Limited/selective (delineated tasks), Open (no specific restrictions but key stages tracked) and Embedded (AI is part of the task). Copying AI output into a submission is not appropriate under the Academic Misconduct Policy, and work must remain the student's own; ask if unsure.
topics.scope: Four-level framework and misconduct policy s4.2-4.5.

claims.text: King's College London suggests four broad levels of generative AI use in assessment that programme and module leaders may adjust to each assessment: Minimal (routine tools such as auto transcription, spell and grammar checkers), Limited/selective (clearly delineated tasks as allowed), Open (no specific restrictions but key stages and tools must be tracked) and Embedded (AI use is a focal part of the assessment). The levels are a framework for the actual assessment brief, not an automatic university-wide permission, and verbatim use of generated content without acknowledgement is never appropriate.

topics.title: Disclosure
topics.summary: Students must acknowledge any generative AI use in coursework with a declaration statement alongside the references, unless the assessment brief gives other wording: either that no part was generated by AI (grammar and spell checking is consistent with this) or that parts have AI contributions within the brief's acceptable use, naming the tools and how they were used. AI is not cited as an authoritative source. Doctoral students choose one of two AI declarations on the RD2 form.

claims.text: King's College London does not require students to cite generative AI as an authoritative source in the reference list, but it requires students to acknowledge any use of generative AI tools in coursework by including a declaration statement with their references. Unless the assessment brief gives other wording, students append either a declaration that no part of the submission was generated by AI software (English grammar and spell checking is consistent with this statement) or a declaration that parts of the submission have AI contributions within the acceptable use specified in the brief, naming the tools and how they were used.

evidence.quote: King’s College London, unlike some other universities, does not require students to reference generative AI as an authoritative source in the reference list for much the same reason you would not be expected to cite a search engine, a student essay website or be over-dependent on synoptic, secondary source material.

topics.title: Research & publication
topics.summary: Doctoral students may use AI in an assistive role to clarify their own writing, including rewriting or paraphrasing parts of the thesis, but not to replace their authorship; AI in the research process itself (e.g. data analysis) falls under research design and ethics review. Uploading research material needs prior written supervisory approval, theses carry an RD2 AI declaration, and examiners must not upload theses to AI or use AI detectors.

claims.text: King's College London permits doctoral students to use generative AI tools in an assistive role in thesis writing, to clarify their own writing and avoid misrepresenting their meaning; this can include rewriting, rephrasing or paraphrasing parts of the thesis. Use beyond the circumstances permitted by the doctoral guidance risks breaching the Academic Misconduct Policy, and AI used in the research process itself (for example to analyse data) is largely outside this guidance and falls under research design, ethical review and research-integrity norms.

evidence.quote: Yes, students are permitted to make use of generative AI tools in their thesis writing processes. However, where a student's use of generative AI tools in their thesis writing exceeds the circumstances permitted by this guidance, they will risk breaching the Academic Misconduct Policy.

additionalTopics.title: Academic integrity & procedures
additionalTopics.summary: Inappropriate, unattributed AI use can be academic misconduct, but poor academic practice (e.g. incomplete citation) is not misconduct. Cases normally start with an informal Academic Integrity Meeting where students may be asked to explain their work but need not give specific answers. A Stage One penalty can be contested within 10 working days of written notification; a Misconduct Committee decision can be appealed within 10 working days on limited grounds. Outcomes range from warnings and capped resubmission to suspension or expulsion. King's has not enabled Turnitin's AI-detection percentage, though similarity checking continues.

claims.text: At King's College London, inappropriate use of generative AI without attribution is considered academic misconduct and can result in penalties ranging from formal warnings to expulsion.

evidence.quote: Inappropriate use without attribution is considered academic misconduct. For further details please see the Academic Misconduct Policy and Academic Misconduct Procedure. Potential penalties can range from formal warnings, resubmitting the coursework, suspension or expulsion.

claims.text: King's Academic Misconduct Policy distinguishes poor academic practice from academic misconduct: an ASB Chair may decide a concern is an unintentional misunderstanding of scholarly practice (for example incomplete citation), which is not misconduct; the student receives feedback and the work is marked against the criteria. Blatant, extensive or careless failures are excluded from this category.

evidence.quote: Once the ASB Chair (or their nominee) has reviewed the information available, they may decide that the concern relates to poor academic practice and that no academic misconduct has occurred. Poor academic practice involves an unintentional misunderstanding of scholarly practice. Examples include when sources are acknowledged to some extent, but citation is inadequate or incomplete. It does not include when the failure to adhere to scholarly practice is blatant, extensive or results from a lack of effort. Poor academic practice is not a form of academic misconduct.

claims.text: Under King's Academic Misconduct Policy, a suspected case normally goes first to a Stage One Academic Integrity Meeting (AIM) with two staff members. The AIM is not a hearing and should be informal, supportive and exploratory; where authorship or third-party involvement is in doubt the student may be asked to explain their answers, ideas or references, but must not be pressured or obliged to give specific responses and may respond in writing instead. Staff share their notes, and the student may add information, normally within 5 working days. Possible Stage One outcomes are no concern, poor academic practice, a local educative or restorative outcome, or referral to a Stage Two Misconduct Committee.

claims.text: King's Academic Misconduct Policy provides two different review routes with different start points. Where a Stage One AIM finds misconduct and applies a local penalty (Outcome 3), the student may send a contestation in writing to Student Conduct & Appeals within 10 working days from the date of written notification of the Stage One outcome. A Stage Two Misconduct Committee decision may be appealed, on the grounds of new evidence or significant procedural error, by submitting a Misconduct Appeal Form within 10 working days of the date of the Misconduct Committee outcome. Possible outcomes range from educative measures such as a formal warning or capped resubmission to punitive outcomes up to suspension or expulsion; AI use does not carry an automatic penalty.

additionalTopics.title: Teaching & course guidance
additionalTopics.summary: King's College London supports considered use of generative AI and is open to evolving teaching, assessment, and feedback practices according to need and disciplinary differences. Institutional guidance for AI-assisted marking and feedback (July 2025) emphasizes that reading and assessing student work should primarily be conducted by humans, with human oversight essential to ensure accuracy and appropriateness. Staff should not use GenAI tools to detect students' use of GenAI, as these tools are notoriously unreliable. Staff should never upload student work or include student details into any AI system or GenAI tool without explicit consent, permission, and forethought; approved or supported university GenAI tools should be used for AI-assisted feedback and marking. This guidance governs staff marking and data handling, and does not set course permissions for students.
